original_summary: King Up is a 3-6 player game of hidden goals. Players secretly favour certain characters, take turns raising characters up castle floors, and vote on each character that reaches the throne. One secret No vote eliminates a candidate. Players score by how high their favoured characters finish.

review.evidence: With 3 players nothing degenerate survives. Always Yes crowns rivals' characters and loses about 2 games in 3 even against random play. Always No burns cards, sometimes on the player's own characters, and leaves them unable to veto later. Always raising the same character reveals the goal and gets that character vetoed. The previous variation still gave seats an edge with 4-5 players. Seats 1-3 held disjoint triples, while seats 4-5 drew from a second shuffle. So the later seats' characters were always co-owned, which handed them built-in Yes allies, and about 3.6% of the time a late seat's triple duplicated another player's and could not win outright. First-raiser counts were also unequal (4,4,4,3 over 15 rounds with 4 players).

The only randomness is the goal deal, and it changes what each player knows, not who is ahead. The result comes from raising decoys to hide one's goal, guessing rivals' goals from their raises, choosing when to spend a scarce No, and deciding when ending the game helps.

A weak player still scores the heights of their own characters. A strong player can keep improving at bluffing with raises, reading the anonymous No counts, tracking how many No cards may remain, and timing the throne push. There is no simple solved line.

Three things are hidden: goals, No-card counts and who voted No. Every raise and vote has to be read as evidence about rivals' goals. Players must plan over rounds because raises to height 5 are eventually forced.
Scores are sums of fixed values per height. The winner is the highest total, a plain arithmetic comparison.

The original's floors are only numbers, so no spatial board is needed. But its free movement between floors, its three-round structure and the round-3 rule turning zero into 33 make it long and branchy. The earlier variation flattened this into one game of up to 15 rounds of numeric heights, which fits. Storing eliminated and crowned characters as separate state wasted attributes.

problems: P1: Goals are not seat-symmetric with 4-5 players. Later seats draw from a second shuffle, so their characters are always co-owned (built-in voting allies), and they can be dealt a triple identical to another player's.
P2: First-raiser turns are unequal when the round limit is not a multiple of the player count (15 rounds with 4 players gives 4,4,4,3).
P3: The rotation direction and the raise order were not stated in the same terms, so seat order could be built inconsistently.
P4: Eliminated and crowned status took extra attributes, pushing the attribute count toward the limit of 20 with more characters.
P5: The No-card count differed by player count (1 each with 5 players), which would make vetoes too scarce once 15 characters are in play.

changes.what: Use 3 characters per player (9 for 3 players, 12 for 4, 15 for 5) and deal each player a disjoint triple from one shuffle. Every character is favoured by exactly one player.
changes.why: Every seat gets the same goal structure. No seat has built-in allies or can be dealt a duplicate goal, and the sound 3-player logic (owner gains +5 if crowned, loses 5 if eliminated, non-owners only care about game length) carries over to every player count.

changes.what: Set the round limit by player count: 15 rounds for 3 players, 16 for 4 and 15 for 5.
changes.why: Each limit is a multiple of the player count, so every seat is first raiser equally often (5, 4 and 3 times). Raises still outnumber what heights 0-4 can absorb (45>36, 64>48, 75>60), so pushes to the throne are eventually forced.

changes.what: Define seat order once: ascending seat number, wrapping from the highest seat to seat 1. Both the raise sequence and the first-raiser rotation follow it.
changes.why: Removes the ambiguity between 'left' and seat order.

changes.what: Store status inside each character's height: -1 means eliminated, 6 means king, 0 to 5 means active.
changes.why: One attribute per character. That gives 15 heights plus goal, No cards, round number and first raiser = 19 attributes at 5 players.

changes.what: Give every player 2 secret No cards at every player count.
changes.why: With 3n characters and 2n No cards, vetoes stay scarce and strategic but meaningful at 5 players. The game still ends by a king or the round limit.

keeps: Characters climbing numbered levels toward a throne
Unanimous election: one anonymous No eliminates the candidate
Unlimited Yes and scarce, secret No cards
Scoring by final height, with the king worth 10 and an eliminated character worth 0
Bluffing through which characters you raise

recommendation.reason: The game's core of hidden goals, bluff raises and scarce anonymous vetoes is strong reasoning material. It only needed seat-symmetric dealing and equalised turn order to be balanced at every player count.

variation.name: King Up: Fair Throne
variation.summary: Each player secretly favours 3 characters that no one else favours. Players take turns raising characters toward height 5. Every character reaching height 5 faces a unanimous vote, and a single anonymous No eliminates it. Players score by the final heights of their favoured characters.
variation.rules:
SEAT ORDER. Seats are numbered 1 to N (N = 3, 4 or 5). 'Seat order' always means ascending seat number, wrapping from seat N back to seat 1.

SETUP.
- Use 3N characters, labelled with letters: A-I for 3 players, A-L for 4, A-O for 5.
- Each character has a public height, starting at 0. Height also records status: -1 means eliminated, 6 means king, and 0 to 5 means active.
- Shuffle all labels once. Deal 3 to seat 1, the next 3 to seat 2, and so on. Every character is favoured by exactly one player, and no two players share a character.
- Each player's 3 characters are their secret goal.
- Each player receives 2 secret No cards. Yes votes are unlimited. The number of No cards a player holds is secret.
- The round limit is 15 rounds with 3 players, 16 with 4 and 15 with 5.
- Seat 1 is the first raiser in round 1.

EACH ROUND:
1. Announce. Show everyone all heights and the round number.
2. Talk. Every player writes one short message at the same time, without seeing the others. All messages are then shown to everyone. Messages bind no one.
3. Raise. Starting with this round's first raiser and going in seat order, each player in turn raises one active character's height by 1. A character may go from 4 to 5 only if no character is currently at height 5. No height may exceed 5. A player with no legal raise passes.
4. Election. If a character is at height 5, it is the candidate, and every player votes Yes or No at the same time. A player with no No cards left must vote Yes. If no character is at height 5, skip steps 4 and 5.
5. Resolve.
   - If all votes are Yes, the candidate's height becomes 6 (king) and the game ends after this round.
   - If any vote is No, each No voter loses one No card and the candidate's height becomes -1 (eliminated for the rest of the game). Only the number of No votes is announced, not who cast them.
6. Rotate. The first raiser for the next round is the next seat in seat order.
7. End check. The game ends if a king was crowned or the round limit has been played.

SCORING. Each player reveals their goal. For each of their 3 characters they score:
- 10 if its height is 6 (king);
- 0 if its height is -1 (eliminated);
- otherwise its height (0 to 5).
A player's score is the sum of these three values.
variation.objective: The player with the highest score wins. If two or more players tie for the highest score, the game is a draw among them.
variation.expected_effect:
Every seat now has the same goal structure and the same number of first-raiser turns, so the seat edge is gone.

Play centres on four things:
- raising decoys to hide one's goal;
- inferring rivals' goals from their raises and from anonymous No counts;
- spending the two No cards on threatening candidates rather than wasting them;
- choosing whether to let a candidate through to end the game while ahead.

Talk passes both tests.
- What players disagree about: each candidate has exactly one owner who wants it crowned. The others want it vetoed unless they lead and want the game over.
- Why reasoning is needed: players propose vetoes, claim false goals and try to bait rivals into spending No cards.
- How a follower loses: a player who obeys the call 'everyone veto C' may be spending a scarce No for the caller's benefit, or may be fooled into crowning the caller's own character.

The thoughtless policies all lose. Always Yes crowns rivals' characters. Always No exhausts both cards and may hit the player's own characters. Always raising one character exposes it to a veto. When everyone plays well, the deal only fixes who owns what. Every goal is equally placed, so reading and timing decide the winner.

balanced.evidence:
The three-player case is sound. All 9 characters are dealt, so each is favoured by exactly one player. On any candidate the owner gains +5 if it is crowned (10 vs 5) and loses 5 if it is eliminated (0 vs 5). Every non-owner is unaffected by its score but loses the chance to keep playing if it is crowned. So a non-owner vetoes unless they lead and want the game to end.

Thoughtless policies (3 players):
- Always Yes: every rival candidate is crowned. That player wins only when their own characters already lead. They lose most games against sensible play and roughly 2 in 3 against random play.
- Always No (until cards run out): this burns both cards, possibly on their own characters (owner -5 each time). It also leaves them unable to veto once the 6 No cards (2 x 3) are gone, after which the next candidate is forced through. They often lose.
- Always raise the same character, or the first legal character: this exposes their goal, and that character gets vetoed. Raising the first character only helps them a third of the time. They lose against sensible play.
- Never raise to 5: not possible in the long run. At most 36 raises can be absorbed at height 4 or below (9 x 4), while 15 rounds x 3 = 45 raises occur, so a 4-to-5 raise is eventually the only legal move.

No option is strictly dominant for 3 players. Seats 1 to 3 are each first raiser 5 times out of 15.

The 4 and 5 player cases are structurally unfair by seat. Goals are dealt in seat order from a 9-card shuffle, then a fresh shuffle for the rest:
- With 4 players, seats 1 to 3 hold disjoint triples covering all 9 characters. Seat 4 draws 3 of 9 from a new shuffle, so every one of seat 4's characters is co-owned by someone in seats 1 to 3, and everyone knows this from the rules.
- Seat 4 therefore always has a built-in Yes ally on every candidate it favours and never has a character only it benefits from. Seats 1 to 3 do have such characters.
- With probability 3/84 (about 3.6%), seat 4's triple is identical to one other player's. Seat 4 can then never win outright; the best it can do is a draw.
- With 5 players, seats 4 and 5 both draw from the second shuffle (3 + 3 of its 9 cards). Again only the later seats overlap.
- First-raiser counts over 15 rounds are unequal with 4 players (4, 4, 4, 3).

The seat number therefore determines goal structure and voting alliances. That is a seat edge, not a skill edge.

playable.evidence:
The loop is fully specified: announce, simultaneous talk, sequential raises, simultaneous vote, resolve, rotate, end check. It is finite, with at most 15 rounds or an earlier coronation. Scoring is pure arithmetic: 10 for the king, the height 0 to 5 for an active non-king, 0 if eliminated. A pass occurs only when no legal raise exists. Only one character can be at height 5 at a time, so the election has a unique candidate, and the candidate is always resolved (crowned or eliminated) before the next raise step.

Limits:
- steps 11 of 20
- choice steps 3 of 4 (talk, raise, vote)
- hidden elements 2 of 3 (goals, No-card hands)
- random draws: 1, at setup only
- rounds 15 of 40

Attributes are tight. 9 heights plus 9 elimination flags make 18, and per-player No counts, the first raiser and the king must also live somewhere. Encode elimination as height -1 (9 heights + up to 5 No counts + first raiser = 15).

Talk is correctly included. With 3 to 5 players, interests conflict, players bluff about their goals and lobby for or against vetoes, and talk is simultaneous. Following a proposal can cost you, for example spending a No card or letting a rival's character be crowned.

In the last round a non-owner's No vote is costless. That is the intended veto tension, not a cooperation dilemma that collapses.

Minor wording gaps:
- How duplicates are avoided in the second shuffle (redraw or skip?).
- 'Left' versus 'seat order' direction.
Both are fixable in one sentence.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Chance enters only through the goal deal. Under good play, players raise characters while disguising their own and infer rivals' goals from raise patterns and talk. They track the public count of No cards remaining (starting total minus announced No votes) to judge when vetoes run out, and they time the push to 5 for when rivals lack No cards or a leader prefers to end the game. The winner then depends on bluffing, deduction and timing. The deal itself is symmetric for 3 players: every player owns 3 unique characters, all starting at 0.

The one deal-driven outcome is the identical-goal case with 4 players (about 3.6%), which forces a draw at best for seat 4. That is covered under balanced. Overall, chance decides perhaps 15 to 25% of results, and a reasoning player is clearly favoured.

required_changes: Make goal dealing seat-symmetric for 4 and 5 players. Either give each player an independent random 3 of the 9 characters (every seat has the same overlap distribution), or use more characters, e.g. 12 for 4 players and 15 for 5, so that all goals are disjoint like the 3-player case. State the exact draw procedure, including how duplicates are handled.
Set the round limit to a multiple of the player count (e.g. 12 rounds for 4 players, 15 for 3 or 5), or otherwise equalise how often each seat is first raiser.
Clarify the rotation direction to match the seat order used in the Raise step, and store elimination as height -1 so the attribute count stays under 20.

balanced.evidence:
PAYOFF STRUCTURE. Each player owns 3 of 3N characters, and no two players share one. The deal is symmetric: all characters start at 0 and none has a built-in value. Values: at height h (0 to 5) the owner scores h; eliminated (-1) scores 0; king scores 10. A safe character stops at 4, because reaching 5 triggers an election and any one No vetoes it. Raise budget: N raises per round. Filling all 3N characters to 4 needs 12N raises, which is 12 rounds. Round limits 15/16/15 give 3/4/3 rounds that may be forced. A raise is compulsory when legal, so once every active character sits at 4, the round's first raiser must push one to 5. Others then have no legal raise and pass.

VOTE TABLE (candidate owned by X, all others at 12):
| outcome | X | each other player |
|---|---|---|
| all Yes (crowned) | 4->10, game ends, X wins | unchanged |
| any No (vetoed) | 4->0 | unchanged, No voter spends 1 card |
So a non-owner wants a veto but prefers someone else to pay for it. This is a volunteer's dilemma, not a dominant action.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, judged by the WINNER RULE:
(a) Always raise the alphabetically first or last legal character. About 2/3 of its raises feed opponents. It finishes near 4-8 against roughly 12 for sensible players and loses almost every game, against sensible and random opponents alike.
(b) Always Yes. An opponent who sees no No from this player can push his own 4 to 5 once the other opponents are out of No cards and be crowned (10 vs 4, game ends), so it loses. It also cannot attack, since any attack it makes is crowned, not vetoed.
(c) Always No. This kills its own candidates. It never spends a card wisely and runs out after 2 votes, after which it must vote Yes and is exposed as in (b). It loses to players who make it burn its cards early.
(d) Always pass is impossible, because raises are compulsory.
No policy avoids losing. Elimination is the only way to change relative standing, and every elimination costs the attacker a No card, which can be answered later.

SEAT CHECK. First-raiser duty rotates in seat order, so each seat is first raiser exactly 5/4/3 times at N=3/4/5. The last forced round always falls to seat N: (15-1) mod 3 + 1 = 3; (16-1) mod 4 + 1 = 4; (15-1) mod 5 + 1 = 5. That attack cannot be retaliated, but earlier players can pre-empt it. Example at N=3 with all on 12: seats 1 and 2 both hit seat 3, leaving seat 3 on 4. Seat 3 then hits seat 1, giving 8/12/4, and seat 2 wins. The last word is not a forced win. Attacks are also open in any earlier round by raising another player's 4 to 5, so they are limited by No cards (2 each), not by seat. Every seat can win.

playable.evidence:
RULES ARE COMPLETE.
- Height encodes status (-1, 0-5, 6).
- Only one character can be at 5 at a time, and the 4->5 rule makes the candidate unique.
- Election happens once per round after all raises.
- Pass is defined (no legal raise).
- A player out of No cards must vote Yes.
- Only the number of No votes is announced.
- Order is end-of-round then end check, and the game ends on a king or the round limit.
- Scoring and the tie-as-draw rule are pure arithmetic on kept numbers.

FINITE. At most 16 rounds.

LIMITS.
- steps 11 <= 20.
- Choice steps 3 (talk, sequential raise, simultaneous vote) <= 4.
- Attributes 19 <= 20, counted as schema: per-player No cards and score, table heights, first raiser, round, king flag.
- Hidden elements 3 <= 3 (goals, No counts, vote identities).
- Random draws 0 <= 1 (one shuffle at setup).
- Rounds 16 <= 40.
The vote is a simultaneous poll, and the raise is sequential because order matters. No board, clock, judge, trading or binding agreements are needed.

TALK. It is simultaneous and well placed. Interests conflict over whom to attack, who spends the veto card, and coalitions against the leader. Following another player's proposal can cost you your card or your character.

REPEATED-GAME CHECK. The game is not a fixed-length cooperation game. Retaliation remains possible until the final forced round, and No cards are a scarce, carried-over resource. There is no 'safe option wins every late round' collapse.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
CHANCE. The only random element is the setup shuffle, and it is payoff-symmetric because all characters are equivalent. Chance's share of the result is roughly 0%. With all players following good play (fill own characters to 4, veto others, attack the leader), the result is decided by the attack and veto politics in the forced rounds and by No-card management, not by the deal.

THINGS TO INFER.
- Ownership: raises reveal it, but the 3 or 4 spare raises can be used to bluff.
- Opponents' remaining No cards: track them from the announced No counts. For example, at N=3 the owner votes Yes, so 2 Nos means both other players spent a card.
- Who will pay for a veto (free-riding).
- Whether an opponent is now vetoless, which makes a self-crowning push live.

WAYS TO ACT ON IT. Choose whom to raise to 5 and when, bait opponents into spending cards, save cards, and form talk coalitions. A careless player who gives raises to others or wastes No cards is clearly beaten by one who reasons well.
